project_scope.note: Ungnadia speciosa and Sapindus drummondii are now canonical clickable local family anchors; Acer negundo remains the major reference form pending its own strict county pass.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start with fruit and leaf arrangement rather than one leaf shape.
family_diagnostics.leaves: Can be opposite or alternate, simple or compound.
family_diagnostics.flowers: Often small or functionally unisexual with a floral disk.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Local learning set spans paired samaras, drupe-like soapberries and 3-valved woody capsules.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Sapindaceae cannot be learned from one leaf arrangement or one fruit type.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: whole plant → high-value structure → reproductive confirmation → tie-breaker
visual_lesson.intro: This family is a great anti-memorization lesson: maple, soapberry and Mexican buckeye look unrelated until the reproductive pattern and fruit diversity click.

steps.title: 1 · Maple side: paired samaras
steps.look_for: Two winged mericarps joined as one paired fruit.
steps.why_it_matters: Boxelder is a maple even though its compound leaves can look ash-like.

steps.title: 2 · Soapberry side
steps.look_for: Alternate pinnate leaves and soapberry fruiting architecture.
steps.why_it_matters: Shows how far the family can depart from the maple gestalt.

steps.title: 3 · Mexican buckeye flower
steps.look_for: Pink flowers on woody growth with pinnate leaves.
steps.why_it_matters: Adds the third major local family form.

steps.title: 4 · Mexican buckeye capsule
steps.why_it_matters: Fruit diversity is the strongest teaching hook for Sapindaceae.

comparisons.title: Boxelder vs ash
comparisons.rule: Acer negundo produces paired samaras; Fraxinus produces single samaras.

comparisons.title: Sapindaceae vs Anacardiaceae
comparisons.rule: Sapindaceae usually lacks resinous sap and commonly has lobed/winged fruit or a floral disk; Anacardiaceae is strongly resinous locally and often drupaceous.

visual_lesson.caveat: Do not treat one fruit or leaf arrangement as universal across Sapindaceae.
